opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, AI has become a pretty central collaborator in how we work on the Model Spec, though maybe not in the way people would first guess. The spec itself is fundamentally a statement of human intent: what we want the models to do, what values and tradeoffs we think are right. That part has to stay anchored in human judgment and deliberation. But the models are incredibly useful at almost every step around that.

One big way is stress-testing. When we draft a principle, we can ask a model to find edge cases, places where two parts of the spec seem to conflict, or scenarios where a literal reading would produce a bad outcome. Models are really good at playing the adversarial reader, and they surface ambiguities we'd otherwise only discover much later, when the behavior shows up in the wild.

Another is checking consistency between what the spec says and what the model actually does. We can generate lots of example prompts tied to specific sections, look at how the model responds, and ask whether that response follows the spec as written. Sometimes the model is wrong, and that's a training signal. Sometimes the spec is unclear or says something we didn't really mean, and that's feedback on the document itself. That loop is one of the most valuable things we have.

They also help with the writing itself: tightening language, suggesting clearer examples, flagging when a section reads differently than we intended. And because the spec is meant to be read by models as well as people, it's useful to see how a model interprets a passage. If it takes away something different from what we meant, that tells us something.

So I'd describe it as AI being a partner in refining, testing, and pressure-testing the spec, while the core decisions about what the models should value stay with people, informed by public input and a lot of internal debate. I think that balance will keep shifting as models get more capable, but the goal is always that the spec reflects what we actually intend, and AI helps us close the gap between intent and behavior.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models can generate prompts tied to spec sections and check whether responses follow the spec, including surfacing problems in new scenarios.

r002.rationale: The candidate says models can identify edge cases and places where parts of the spec conflict, surfacing ambiguities that might otherwise be discovered later.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's been surprisingly useful, and in ways I didn't fully anticipate when we started. The Model Spec is this fairly long document that tries to lay out how we want the models to behave: what they should prioritize, how to handle conflicts between the developer, the user, and our own policies, where the lines are. Writing something like that by hand, you end up with a lot of blind spots. You write a principle that sounds clean in the abstract, and then it turns out it contradicts another principle three pages later, or it just doesn't say anything about a whole category of situations that actually come up.

So one of the first things we do now is use the models as a kind of adversarial reader. We'll take a draft section and ask, what's ambiguous here? Give me ten cases where two reasonable people would read this differently. And it's good at that. It'll surface edge cases that none of us had thought about, because it has seen so many different kinds of conversations and it can just enumerate them quickly. That's something humans are pretty bad at doing exhaustively.

The second thing, which I think is more interesting, is that the models help us test whether the spec actually does what we think it does. You can write a rule, then generate a bunch of realistic prompts that stress it, and look at how a model trained with that guidance behaves. If the behavior is wrong, that's a signal the spec was unclear or we were wrong about what we wanted. It closes the loop. The document stops being a philosophy essay and becomes something you can actually evaluate against.

And then there's just the editing. Making the language precise, making sure an example really illustrates the point, noticing when we've used the same word to mean two different things. That's unglamorous, but it matters a lot for a document that's supposed to be read by both people and models.

What I'd push back on is the idea that the AI is writing the spec. The hard part is the judgment calls: what should the default be, whose instructions win, how much weight to put on user autonomy versus safety. Those are human decisions, and they should be. The model is very good at showing us the consequences of a choice and very bad at telling us which choice is right. I think that division of labor is roughly what you want.

r001.rationale: The response says models can test whether the spec works as intended by generating realistic prompts that stress its rules and examining model behavior.

r002.rationale: The response says models can reveal edge cases people had not considered, including where principles may conflict or leave situations uncovered.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can be useful both in helping us write the Model Spec and in helping us test it. When you’re writing down how you want a model to behave, it’s easy to have principles that sound reasonable individually but come into tension in a particular conversation. An AI can help surface those cases: Where is this ambiguous? Where do these two instructions conflict? What have we left unspecified?

Then you can turn those questions into concrete examples and ask whether the behavior you get is actually what you intended. That makes the process much more iterative—you refine the spec, test it, and learn from the gaps.

But there’s still a human judgment at the center. AI can help us understand the consequences of a choice; it doesn’t settle what we ought to choose.

r001.rationale: The response says to turn questions about the spec into concrete examples and test whether the model’s behavior matches the intended behavior.

r002.rationale: It says AI can surface cases where principles come into tension, instructions conflict, or the spec is ambiguous or unspecified.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can be useful at several points in that process. You can ask a model to look for ambiguities or contradictions in the spec, or to generate examples where two principles seem to pull in different directions. Those concrete cases are often much easier to reason about than an abstract rule.

Then you can use models to help evaluate whether actual responses line up with what the spec says. That gives you a feedback loop: sometimes the model needs improvement, and sometimes the spec needs to be clearer.

But I’d distinguish helping us reason about the spec from deciding what it should say. The underlying choices—what behavior we want, how we balance competing values—still need human judgment and input.

r001.rationale: It says models can evaluate whether actual responses align with the Spec, but does not clearly say to apply the Spec to new cases to assess whether it works as intended.

r002.rationale: It says models can generate examples where principles pull in different directions, but does not clearly identify surfacing previously unconsidered interactions between principles.
